storyboard.claim: Will is confident he already knows the story of his father's death.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will in the elevator, chin up, smirking — the boy who has rehearsed this lore his whole life.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pop has just appeared on floor 5; Will responds with bravado.
storyboard.addedInformation: The smirk signals false certainty, setting up the reveal that follows.

storyboard.claim: Pop reveals Will knows only how his father died, not why.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Pop's sorrowful ghost facing Will, the word HOW isolated between them.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Will's confidence is immediately undercut by Pop's secret.
storyboard.addedInformation: The split between HOW and WHY is the structural hinge of this act.

storyboard.claim: The true reason behind his father's death destroys Will's entire family mythology.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will crumpling slightly — the weight of a collapsed story falling on him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Extends the HOW/WHY split: the WHY is not a clarification, it is demolition.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the abstract set reinforces the 'void between beats' of the verse novel.

storyboard.claim: Will constructed a false image of his father to justify his mission.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The mask icon — a curated face, not the real one — beside Will's blank, inward stare.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why the collapse of mythology hits so hard: Will built it on purpose.
storyboard.addedInformation: Mask reads as 'a false public face, pretending' — here Will is pretending to himself.

storyboard.claim: Pop did exactly what Will is about to do: he followed the three rules and sought revenge.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Rules list icon beside the walking ghost of Pop — he obeyed the code.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pop's story begins; the parallel with Will's plan is made explicit.
storyboard.addedInformation: Walk reads as following a path — Pop is moving toward his revenge.

storyboard.claim: Pop pulled the trigger and killed the wrong man.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Gun icon — the instrument of the act — beside Pop standing blank, unable to process what he did.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pop followed the rules to completion; the twist lands here.
storyboard.addedInformation: Blank face = apathy/numbness — the dissociated state after an irreversible act.

storyboard.claim: Will is completely sure Rigs killed Shawn — his entire plan rests on that certainty.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will's confident smirk — a mirror of Pop's certainty before he fired.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The parallels Pop–Will now include shared certainty about who the guilty man is.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the smirk echo sets up the horror of 128 without naming it.

storyboard.claim: Will's justification for murder is built entirely on unverified certainty.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will still talking himself into it — the smirk now reads as dangerous, not charming.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Doubles down on 126 — the repetition is deliberate, stressing how fragile this foundation is.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: two consecutive smirk/talk beats are intentional — the host is holding on this point.

storyboard.claim: Pop was equally certain, followed the code, orphaned a child, died — all over mistaken identity.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Pop slumped on the street set, the weight of what certainty cost him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pop's certainty mirrored Will's in 126–127; the outcome is now visible.
storyboard.addedInformation: Street set = where the wrong shooting happened; slump = the crushing aftermath.

storyboard.claim: Grief makes the brain see only the evidence that confirms its rage.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will thinking, expression worried — the brain turning inward in grief, blind to other evidence.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The analytical pivot: why Pop was certain, why Will is certain.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the abstract set suits an explanatory aside about cognitive science.

storyboard.claim: In grief you see only what justifies your rage — Pop's ghost is the living proof.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Pop's slumped ghost — the embodiment of seeing what you need and getting it catastrophically wrong.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Confirmation bias (129) is now personified in Pop's body.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the viewer feels Pop's agony through his posture, not just the words.

storyboard.claim: Pop describes the physical agony before he sought revenge — his heart stabbing him from inside.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Pop slumped and sad — the visceral internal wound of grief rendered in posture.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from cognitive bias to the bodily experience of grief that preceded the act.
storyboard.addedInformation: The poetic imagery from the verse novel comes through in the callout's concrete brutality.

storyboard.claim: The grief consumed Pop so completely he could no longer be a father or a brother.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Pop still slumped — identity dissolved, only the ghost remaining.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The internal damage (131) becomes a social one: he loses his roles as a person.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: three consecutive slump/sad beats for Pop mirror the cumulative weight of the narration.

storyboard.claim: Trauma does not just make you sad — it destroys your ability to connect with the living.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will and Pop standing apart, both blank — two people who cannot reach each other across the grief.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Generalizes Pop's corruption into a thesis about trauma.
storyboard.addedInformation: The twoShot with blank expressions shows disconnection without staging it symbolically.

storyboard.claim: Pop abandoned Will and Shawn — his living children — for the ghost of his dead brother.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Pop slumped with Will behind him — the son who was sacrificed, present but unreached.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Translates the identity corruption into the specific cost: two sons without a father.
storyboard.addedInformation: Will in the background makes the sacrifice literal — the viewer sees who was left.

storyboard.claim: One host interprets Pop's tragedy as violating rule three by shooting the wrong person.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will thinking — the host's interpretation framed as Will processing a lesson.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The host introduces their reading before the other host refutes it in 137.
storyboard.addedInformation: This is the setup for the debate; the callout frames the wrong conclusion so it can be demolished.

storyboard.claim: The host argues it was user error — if you follow the rules, get the right guy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will smirking — the callous framing of the rules as a tool that only needs correct operation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The cynical reading of 135 made explicit: the rules were fine, Pop just botched the execution.
storyboard.addedInformation: The smirk reads as sinister here — the viewer senses this framing is being set up to be destroyed.

storyboard.claim: The other host rejects the user-error reading: Reynolds's point is the exact opposite.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mark's ghost, surprised — his presence signals who will deliver the counter-argument.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Hard pivot from 136; the debate structure becomes explicit.
storyboard.addedInformation: Mark is on screen because he IS the genius of what Reynolds is doing — the character proves the rebuttal.

storyboard.claim: Pop's tragedy is not that he broke the rules — it's that he executed them perfectly.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Pop standing blank and still — the picture of a man who did everything right by the code.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Directly inverts 136 — the tragedy is not user error but perfect execution.
storyboard.addedInformation: Blank = apathy / numbness; here it reads as the deadened state of a man who did the 'right' wrong thing.

storyboard.claim: Perfect rule-following still killed a completely innocent man and got Pop killed.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Pop slumped on the street — the site of the perfect, catastrophic execution.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The cost of flawless execution (138): innocence destroyed, self destroyed.
storyboard.addedInformation: Street set = the corner where the murder happened; slump = the outcome for Pop.

storyboard.claim: The failure is not in the man who followed the rules — it is in the system itself.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A sorter diagram: MAN vs SYSTEM — the structural verdict the hosts are making.
storyboard.onScreenText: The man vs. the system — where the blame actually belongs.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Closes the debate arc: user error is wrong; the rules themselves are the failure.
storyboard.addedInformation: The diagram is the clearest way to show that two categories are being separated — this is a structural insight.

storyboard.claim: The rules require no proof, no trial — just a body to balance the psychological ledger.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mark angry, delivering the verdict on the rules — any body satisfies the code.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Extends the system critique (140): the rules don't even require the right target.
storyboard.addedInformation: The callout's bluntness mirrors the rules' own bluntness — the horror is in the plainness.

storyboard.claim: The rules don't deliver justice — they multiply blind violence. That is their ultimate failure.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Rules icon — the antagonist of the story, named — beside Mark's angry indictment.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The system critique peaks: the rules are not just flawed, they make things worse.
storyboard.addedInformation: theRules icon here is the visual climax of the argument that began at beat 140.

storyboard.claim: Uncle Mark, the ghost on floor 4, completely shifts the dynamic of the elevator.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The floor counter icon — floor 4 — and Mark walking in, tall, taking up space.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transition: from the verdict on the rules to the introduction of the character who attacks them structurally.
storyboard.addedInformation: floorCounter grounds the abstract analysis back in the elevator's countdown structure.

storyboard.claim: Until now the ghosts have shown Will the consequences of the rules; Mark will attack the structure itself.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will thinking, worried — processing everything he has seen so far before the mode shifts.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Recap beat: the first phase of the elevator journey before Mark changes the game.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: Will's worried-think reads as the burden of accumulated witness.

storyboard.claim: Uncle Mark doesn't show Will consequences — he attacks the structure of the violence itself.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mark smirking, tall and charismatic — the man who will prosecute the rules as a system.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Contrasts with 144: the mode shift from showing consequences to attacking structure.
storyboard.addedInformation: Smirk = sinister charm, the predator smiling — Mark has an edge the other ghosts lack.

storyboard.claim: Mark's casual gesture — tucking a cigarette behind his ear — announces his cool authority.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mark idle, smirking — the cigarette gesture establishes his unhurried, director's confidence.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Character texture after the structural announcement — Mark is comfortable, in control.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: a brief character beat before the technique is named in 147–148.

storyboard.claim: Mark treats the elevator like a movie set, literally directing Will: 'Let's set the scene.'
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mark pointing — the director's gesture — with Will as his reluctant actor.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The cigarette gesture (146) leads into the directing stance — now it is explicit.
storyboard.addedInformation: Point reads as directing/accusation; paired with smirk it reads as sinister authority.

storyboard.claim: Mark is using narrative distance — a trauma therapy technique — to force Will outside his own plan.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mark talking, the abstract set behind him — the technique is being named and explained.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the psychological tool Mark is deploying with his 'set the scene' instruction.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: abstract set fits the analytical register of this explanatory beat.

storyboard.claim: Mark forces Will to see his murder plan from the outside — as a script he is writing.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mark pointing at Will, who looks worried — forced into the observer's chair.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The technique (148) is now in action: Will is being made to narrate his plan.
storyboard.addedInformation: Worried face on Will: the perspective shift is already uncomfortable.

storyboard.claim: Will plays along, narrating his plan — finding the gun, the elevator, finding Rigs — until he stops.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will talking, expression blank — reciting the script of his own plan as if from outside it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Will enacts what Mark demanded in 149 — the narration is happening.
storyboard.addedInformation: Blank = numbness/indifference; Will is dissociating from his own plan as he speaks it.

storyboard.claim: Will stops at the moment of shooting and says nothing. That silence is the trap.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Will frozen, afraid — he has no ending for his own movie and he knows it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The narration of 150 hits the wall: Will cannot finish the script.
storyboard.addedInformation: Afraid face = terror; idle = frozen, stopped. The stopping is the revelation.

storyboard.claim: To understand Mark's chilling response, you must know he used to be an artist.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mark standing, expression neutral — introducing a new layer of who he was before.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pause after the trap springs in 151; now the context for Mark's expertise is established.
storyboard.addedInformation: Neutral face is appropriate here — the narrator is setting up backstory, not making an emotional point yet.

storyboard.claim: Mark's mother bought him a camera for his 18th birthday — he had a whole other life in mind.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mark holding a photo, sad — the lost life captured in an image, a filmmaker who never got to film.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Mark as artist (152) becomes concrete: the camera, the birthday, the stolen future.
storyboard.addedInformation: Photo icon + hold photo = a camera and a record of what was; sad face = grief for the lost path.

storyboard.claim: Mark was a creator forced by economic reality and the gravity of the neighborhood into selling drugs.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mark on the street — the place that pulled him away from filmmaking and toward his death.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The camera and dream (153) collide with the street that swallowed it.
storyboard.addedInformation: Street set = the neighborhood that shaped and destroyed him; sad = grief for the life not lived.

storyboard.claim: Selling, forced by the neighborhood, led to Mark's death — ending the artist's life entirely.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mark slumped on the street — the endpoint of the trajectory from camera to corner to grave.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Closes the backstory arc: the neighborhood forced him, and it killed him.
storyboard.addedInformation: Slump = the dead weight of a life foreclosed.

storyboard.claim: Because Mark was a filmmaker, he understands narrative arcs — and that is why his role in the elevator is so powerful.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mark talking to Will, smirking — the director explaining to his actor why the script matters.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The backstory (153–155) now pays off: the camera explains the technique.
storyboard.addedInformation: Smirk = sinister charm — Mark uses his art knowledge with a director's cold precision.

storyboard.claim: One host reads Mark as trying to remind Will of his humanity — look at this ugly script you're writing.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mark pointing, worried — the moral compass reading: look at what you're becoming.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the first host's interpretation of Mark's role before the other host rejects it.
storyboard.addedInformation: Worried face on Mark = genuine care, not just cold technique — supporting the moral compass reading.

storyboard.claim: The other host rejects that reading — Mark is not a moral compass reminding Will of his humanity.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mark smirking — the colder, more calculating face that the second host sees.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The strike callout rejects 157's interpretation; Mark's smirk confirms the colder reading.
storyboard.addedInformation: Strike style = the narrator rejects the phrase. Smirk = sinister charm replaces worried care.

storyboard.claim: Mark is a director exposing a fatal plot hole in Will's script — when Will says 'the end,' Mark chuckles.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mark smirking at Will — the director who sees exactly where the script breaks.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The colder reading (158) is now specified: Mark is diagnosing a structural failure in Will's narrative.
storyboard.addedInformation: The chuckle is the most chilling detail — Mark is not horrified, he is recognizing a predictable flaw.
